paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I'm actually early, so we'll wait another two minutes.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay. Thank you, Veronica, for leading yoga today, and thank you for your presentation today. So we're going to meditate. We're going to continue to follow the meditation we started yesterday. The idea of these meditations — I want to give a little bit of a talk about it first, and then we'll go ahead and do it. I'll give you a little explanation first, and then we'll start the meditation.

chapters.title: Geshe Michael's Preface — An Introduction to Seeing Emptiness

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: How many people — I know Brian asked this yesterday, but I'm going to ask it again. How many people have read Geshe Michael's Preface? The Preface. One, two, three, four, five, six. Okay.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Do we have that in Taiwanese traditional Chinese characters yet?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: It's cooking.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Is it going to be finished tomorrow?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: I started cooking today.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay, all right. Never mind. So you'll get a copy of that in October. And in it — it's the introduction to a book he's publishing in October called The Illumination of the True Thought.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Illumination of the True Thought — is that the same Geshe Michael’s text that we're using for this course?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: No. I forgot what it's called.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Don't worry about what it's called.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: No, we've got what it's called. What it's called is one of the greatest explanations of emptiness by Je Tsongkapa. It's like a thousand pages. If you have trouble sleeping, you can either take the herbs that Janet gave you — what she gave me last night — or you can just open up a couple of pages of that book, and then you'll fall asleep. Although I tend to have a weird reaction when I read emptiness things — it actually wakes me up. Brian's laughing; he's the same. Yeah, it's weird. If I do too much of it, I get, like, energized.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So that explanation of emptiness — Geshe Michael wrote an introduction to it called the Preface. In English, "preface" is a fancy word for "introduction." So it's the Preface — the introduction — which I think is really cool. And we're giving this book away to everyone around the world for free. It's kind of a genius title, because it's an introduction to how to see emptiness directly. And it's written from a first-person point of view, from Geshe Michael's point of view — based on his direct experience: what happened before, during, and after that experience. His goal in writing it, as far as I understand, is to help us understand the seeds we really need to plant to generate that experience.

chapters.title: The Four Arya Truths and the Sixteen Aspects

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Just briefly: when you see emptiness directly, there are four main realizations you have, which we call the Four Arya Truths. Four very, very clear ideas come to you. The first one is — what? Suffering. Everything is suffering — meaning everything that has a beginning has an end. Even good things end. What's the second one? There's a cause to the suffering; there's a reason for it. What's the third?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Cessation?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Let's use a different word — "cessation" is so boringly philosophical. There's an end. There's an end to suffering; suffering can end. And what's the fourth one called? The path — there's a way. Which means there's a cause. So there's suffering, there's a cause for it, there's an end to it, and there's a cause for that end.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Each of those four truths has four parts each. So when you have that realization, you actually have four realizations for each of the truths. So in the Preface — in that introduction — he describes all sixteen of those parts. And there isn't a whole lot of description of those sixteen parts in any of the Buddhist literature from the Buddha's time on. So he's providing a commentary to it, based on his own experience. And not only that — he's going to teach us how to plant the seeds to have all sixteen of those. He started teaching us that in Malaysia, and he's continuing on that theme, and we're going to continue with it in these meditations.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So the first step he's teaching us is: how do we look at the life we have — the life we received when we were born? How do we see why what happened to us happened to us? We're doing an investigation into our younger years — looking at things that happened to us, things we were attracted to, things we enjoyed, our family, our culture — and asking: what seeds had to have been planted to create that? So it's a personal investigation, going back into the story of your life.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There's a song called "The Story of My Life." Anyway — the point is, each of us is going to be investigating our own stories. This is how I think about my meditation in the morning; this is what gets me up in the morning.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The idea is that we're going to do different themes, and just investigate. Yesterday, what did we do?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: The teachers.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Right — before twelve years old, the teachers. I was waiting for the only word in there I'd understand: "teachers." I was meditating earlier and forgot to turn it off, so I got extra minutes. We looked at the teachers we had when we were younger, and then tried to say, "okay, what seeds did I plant?"

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So today's theme is a little different, and you haven't done this one yet. If you were in Malaysia, you did the teacher one. We were just warming up yesterday, but we'll continue investigating.
